Just now

My cousin in Lahore sent me a screenshot of a conversation with intelligence three months ago. He had asked the intelligence to write a business plan and got three paragraphs of generic nonsense back. He was frustrated. He said artificial intelligence was overrated.
I asked my cousin one question: what did you tell the intelligence about your business? He had typed eleven words. That is the problem there. Most people treat intelligence like a mind reader. They type a sentence. Expect magic. Then when they get an answer they blame the artificial intelligence instead of the way they asked.
I have spent six months using artificial intelligence daily for writing, research, coding help and business ideas. Along the way I made every mistake you can make. This guide is everything I wish someone had told me on day one whether you are sitting in New York, London or Karachi.
What does talking to intelligence actually mean? Forget the name for a second. Talking to intelligence just means talking to artificial intelligence the way you would brief a smart new employee.
Imagine you hire someone brilliant. They have never met you do not know your business. Have zero context about what you want. If you just say write something they will guess. Guessing rarely produces work.
Imagine you instead say: write a two hundred word Instagram caption for a candle brand targeting women aged twenty five to thirty five in the United States, warm and slightly playful tone include one call to action. Different result. Same employee, brain, but now they actually know what you need.
Artificial intelligence works the way. It is not reading your mind. It is reading your words.
I use a trick now before sending any prompt. I read it back. I ask myself: could a stranger who knows nothing about my situation understand what I want from this? If the answer is no I rewrite it.
A friend of mine in Toronto runs a store. She used to type things like help me write product descriptions. The artificial intelligence gave her copy every time.
Then she changed her approach. She started writing: I sell leather wallets for men aged twenty five to forty. Write a product description in a no fluff tone focus on durability and everyday use keep it under eighty words. Same artificial intelligence. Same store. Different quality of output.
The lesson here is not complicated. Specific instructions produce results. Vague instructions produce results.
I break every prompt down into four parts now. I call it my checklist.
* Role: who should the artificial intelligence act as? A teacher, a copywriter, a career coach, an advisor?
* Context: what is the situation? Who is the audience? What is the goal?
* Task: what do you want done? Be specific about format, length and tone.
* Constraints: any rules it should follow? Word count, style things to avoid?
Here is an example that shows all four working together. Act as a career coach. I am a twenty four year software engineer from Islamabad applying for remote jobs at companies based in the United States and the United Kingdom. Write a LinkedIn summary that highlights my Python and web development skills without sounding boastful. Keep it under one hundred and fifty words.
Compare that to typing write me a LinkedIn bio. You already know which one gets results.
When I first started I thought longer prompts always meant results. So I would write these paragraphs stuffed with every detail I could think of.
Turns out that is not it either. The real skill is not writing prompts. It is writing prompts. Sometimes clarity means adding detail. Sometimes it means cutting the noise.
A designer I know in Manchester once told me something that stuck with me. She said, I do not need intelligence to know everything about my life. I need it to know what this one task requires.
That is the mindset shift. Stop treating intelligence like a diary. Start treating it like a tool that needs a brief.
There is this idea floating around that you need secret power prompts to get results. Special phrases, words, tricks nobody else knows.
Honestly I do not buy it anymore. What actually moves the needle is context. The relevant background you give the intelligence the better it performs. Not tricks. Just clarity.
Think about it like ordering food. If you walk into a restaurant and say give me something you might get lucky. If you say I want something vegetarian and under five hundred calories you will get exactly what you need almost every time.
Artificial intelligence works the way. Context is the difference between a guess and a reliable answer.
Here is something interesting I have noticed. In the United States or the United Kingdom most people already assume artificial intelligence tools like ChatGPT are accessible, fast and part of workflow. In Pakistan and much of South Asia there is still hesitation. Some of it comes from exposure. Some comes from payment barriers since many artificial intelligence tools require credit cards that’re not always easy to access locally.
Here is the good news. The skill of prompting does not depend on where you live. Whether you are using a paid tool in California or a free version in Karachi the principles stay the same. Clear role context, task, clear constraints.
I have seen freelancers in Lahore use these techniques to write cover letters that landed them clients in the United States and Canada. The artificial intelligence tool did not care about their location. It cared about the clarity of their instructions.
Time you use artificial intelligence for anything writing an email planning a trip brainstorming a business idea try this. Write your prompt the way you normally would. Save the response.
Then rewrite it using the four part method: role, context, task, constraints. Compare the two answers side by side.
I did this exercise with my resume summary a while back. My first attempt got me a paragraph. My second attempt, using context about my industry and target job got me something I could genuinely use without editing.
The difference was not the intelligence getting smarter. It was me getting clearer.
The real skill nobody talks about is communication. The people who get the results from intelligence tools are usually the same people who are good at explaining things to other humans. They know how to set context. They know how to be specific without over explaining. They know what done well actually looks like before they ask for it.
If you are someone who struggles with instructions from your boss or someone who has ever had to explain a task because the first explanation was not clear enough that same skill applies here.
Getting good at intelligence is not a technical skill. It is a clarity skill.
Start small. Pick one task you do regularly an email, a caption, a summary and practice writing prompts for it this week.
Do not aim for perfect. Aim for specific.
The gap between people who feel frustrated with intelligence and people who feel like it is genuinely useful almost always comes down to this one thing. Not access to tools. Not living in a country with resources. Just knowing how to ask.
My cousin in Lahore the one, with the eleven word tried again a week later. This time he gave the intelligence his business idea, his target market, his budget and what kind of plan he actually needed.
He sent me the version. It was not perfect. It was actually useful.
That is the point.
